data.abstract: Human sleep which can be measured by polysomnography consists of two major states, the Rapid-Eye-Movement (REM) sleep and the non-REM sleep. Non-REM sleep is characterised by increasing EEG synchronisation and divided into stages 1 to 4. Stages 3 and 4 are defined as slow-wave sleep (SWS). Typical nocturnal sleep is characterised by 3 to 5 cycles of non-REM- and REM-sleep phases that last about 60 to 100 minutes. At the beginning of the night the cycles contain more SWS. Towards the end of the night, the amount of REM sleep increases and the amount of SWS decreases. The pattern of nocturnal growth hormone (GH) secretion is associated with the development of SWS during the first non-REM-sleep period. By contrast, cortisol secretion appears to be associated with an increased amount of REM sleep. At least three major processes are involved in the regulation of normal sleep. According to the two-process model of sleep regulation, sleep and wakefulness are influenced by both a homoeostatic and a circadian process: the homoeostatic process S - related to SWS - increases with the duration of wakefulness prior to sleep onset and augments sleep propensity. The circadian process C describes the daily cycle of sleepiness and wakefulness and is related to REM sleep. The third process is the ultradian rhythm of non-REM and REM sleep. The non-REM/REM sleep cycle is regulated within the brain stem: REM sleep is initiated and maintained by cholinergic neurons and is inhibited by noradrenergic and serotonergic neurons. In contrast to the brain-stem-activated state of REM sleep, non-REM sleep is characterised by synchronised, rhythmic inhibitory-excitatory potentials in large numbers of neurons in cortical and thalamic regions. Although specific sleep patterns are not necessarily diagnostic of particular psychiatric disorders, there are relationships between certain sleep abnormalities and categories of psychiatric disorders. Especially, in the majority of depressed patients severe sleep disturbances as reflected by disturbed sleep maintenance, a deficit of SWS, an earlier onset of the first REM-sleep period (shortened REM latency) and increased density of REMs during REM sleep (REM density) are well-established findings. Some of them also persist in the fully remitted state and are thus believed to be trait like. The importance of sleep in depression is also supported by many studies showing that total and partial sleep deprivation or selective REM-sleep deprivation has antidepressant effects. Inspired by the growing knowledge of the neurobiology of sleep, investigators proposed theories into the pathophysiology of depression. The models have attempted to explain the features of sleep in depression and the antidepressant effects of sleep deprivation in depressed patients. The cholinergic-aminergic imbalance hypothesis of depression assumes that the cycling alternating pattern of non-REM and REM sleep is under the control of noradrenergic/serotonergic and cholinergic neuronal networks. If depression results from diminished noradrenergic and serotonergic neurotransmission, cholinergic activity would be expected to increase and therefore lead to the sleep disturbances in depression. Further, there is evidence that sleep regulation and depression share common pathophysiological mechanisms at the serotonergic level. According to the two-process model of sleep regulation depression is thought to result from a deficiency in the process S. In the extended two-process model the interaction of hormones with EEG features has been integrated: GH releasing hormone (GHRH) is a common stimulus of SWS and GH release, whereas corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) exerts opposite effects.
